brief.head: One fry fits all
brief.text: Industrial food homogenises, Ajay Shah said, down to one potato for McDonald’s fries. “It is impossible to think deeply about the health system without thinking deeply about the food system.” {012-C13}

brief.head: Islands of caste
brief.text: Ajay Shah compared India’s endogamous groups to island ecosystems. Endogamy, said Amit Varma, citing David Reich, left India “full of many different thousands of small populations”. {012-C10}

brief.head: Two tongues per boy
brief.text: Migrant men formed families with local women, so a boy spoke his mother’s tongue first, then the men’s. Amit Varma found that in Peggy Mohan’s *Wanderers, Kings, Merchants*. {012-R26}

brief.head: Brides on the move
brief.text: Outside elite circles, Amit Varma said, women who marry and move almost start from scratch. Chinmay Tumbe found that marriage is the largest source of internal migration in India. {012-C11}

brief.head: Too warm to rise
brief.text: Dahi likes India’s heat, Ajay Shah said, but sourdough needs about 20°C. Hence a culture of unleavened roti and naan, with khamiri roti the northern exception. {012-C14}

thought.text: May you have peace in your life, but ferment in your food.

lead.kicker: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah on where ‘Indian’ comes from
lead.head: A khichdi called culture
body: Amit Varma came dressed in a Patiala salwar, and Ajay Shah asked him about the Indian look. Varma rejected the label. Stitched clothing came from outside, he said, and his salwar is of Middle Eastern origin.

That set the theme. Almost nothing thought of as quintessentially Indian started here. Potatoes, chillies, tomatoes and guava came from South America. Marigolds came from Mexico; saffron probably arrived via the Middle East; even idli fermentation may have come from Indonesia.
“You can make the narrow argument that nothing is really Indian so we shouldn’t call anything Indian per se,” Varma said. “But my broader argument would be that everything is Indian.” {012-C01}
Once influences arrive, Varma argued, they are ours. Language, food and clothes are at their best mixed: “The best things are always a khichdi, a delightful mixture.” {012-C02}
Even English counts. It borrows from Greek, Persian, Anglo-Saxon and Hindustani, Varma said, so it is an Indian language, and arguably not even an English one.
## Both ways

Trade always ran in two directions. Varma read from Pushpesh Pant’s *India: Cookbook*: “The traders brought with them the culinary secrets of leavened bread, baking, and noodles. In return, the Indians introduced the Europeans to the joys of curry, mangoes and chutney.” {012-C03}
Shah’s favourite tale of the Columbian Exchange was the potato, which travelled from South America and, under Frederick the Great, reshaped the logistics of European armies.
## Sameness sets in

Mixing has a dark twin, homogenisation. Varma’s example, from the food writer Vikram Doctor, is the Cavendish banana. India gave bananas to the world; Latin America reduced them to one dull yellow strain and sent it back, and India’s own varieties are dying out. {012-S03}
Weddings everywhere, Pushpesh Pant complains, have one Punjabi stall and one chowmein stall. Shah blamed industrial food, which wants a single standard product, and swore off basmati rice for good.
Mass media did the same to language, Shah argued. Television and films gave America one standard accent, and the state’s promotion of Hindi replaced the diverse Hindustani of 75 years ago.

Both hosts see the tide turning. Varma pointed to Stage, which streams in Haryanvi and Bhojpuri; in a long tail, you don’t need economies of scale. Shah pointed to YouTube, where people “discover Konkani shows”. {012-C06}
## Ours to remix

Varma’s model of a cuisine has two stages: local conditions first, from produce and climate to fuel, class and caste, then a mixture of outside influences. A rice shortage gave the South upma; cow dung’s slow flame made Indian cooking a matter of boiling.
Shah pleaded for saving inherited knowledge, like his mother’s recipe for the dal Osaman, while it still exists. But culture, he said, must not be “a fly in the amber”.

Varma called cultural appropriation an incoherent idea: “If it’s cultural, how can there be appropriation?” Shah told how Rabindranath Tagore’s heirs insisted his works be performed as in his time, and called it a tragedy.
Culture, Shah said, is the software of Homo sapiens, and software can be rewritten. Varma had a shorter definition, which he proposed naming the show after: “Everything is everything.”

second.label: Food and labour
second.head: Upma, a wartime truce
second.deck: Amit Varma relays Krish Ashok’s theory of rice, rotis and women’s time
body: Krish Ashok has a theory, Amit Varma said, about why more women worked and more girls went to school in South India. Among many factors, the South ate rice, cooked in one batch, while rotis took hours of labour every day. {012-S05}

Then rice ran short. Varma thought it was during the Second World War, around the Japanese invasion of Burma. Orders came from above telling the South to eat more wheat, backed by wheat promotion campaigns. {#wheat}

But the women were working and the girls were at school, and nobody wanted to sit around all day making rotis. Their answer was a kind of wheat that cooks like rice. “And that is the origin of Semolina Upma,” Varma said.

quote.text: So they came up with a compromise, which was a kind of wheat that can be cooked like rice, semolina.

second.caption: the origin of upma

third.head: High rents, safe menus
body: Five years ago, the food writer Vikram Doctor told Amit Varma that Bombay restaurants were bad. The reason, he said, was rent. {012-S07}

“When you invest so much in opening a restaurant, you cannot experiment with a niche or with something experimental,” Varma said, recalling Doctor’s answer. So the city got Udupi joints and paneer butter masala, which put Varma in mind of Pratap Bhanu Mehta, “because he’s called PBM”. {012-J10}
Varma saw the same logic in Indian FM radio. Licences cost hundreds of crores and political news was not allowed, so stations had no option but Bollywood and popular music. {#fm}
Had he pitched *The Seen and the Unseen*, or a show with “my friend Ajay Shah the card carrying economist”, he said, they would have laughed him out of the room. Podcasting changed that.
third.caption: why Bombay restaurants were bad

p2.title: Everything is Indian
p2.deck: How food, language and culture travel, mix and settle, as argued over by Amit Varma and Ajay Shah

sections.label: From elsewhere
sections.head: Marigolds from Mexico
sections.caption: food that came from elsewhere
body: Almost everything we think of as Indian food is from somewhere else, Amit Varma said, whether it is rajma chawal or tandoori chicken. Potatoes, chillies, tomatoes and guava arrived from South America in what is called the Columbian Exchange. {012-C03}
Exchange ran both ways. In Pushpesh Pant’s account, one of Vasco da Gama’s shipments alone carried fifteen hundred tons of pepper, along with ginger, cinnamon and cloves. {#pepper}

Vikram Doctor told Varma that the marigold, so common at weddings, comes from Mexico. {#marigold} Saffron grows in colder climates and probably reached India via the Middle East; in India, only Kashmir has the right temperature for it.
## Wangi to eggplant

When the writer Soity Banerjee recreated an Indus Valley meal, the only ingredient we would recognise, as Varma remembered it, was baingan. What you call it, he joked, measures your distance from a Maharashtrian village. Say “wangi” and you are close; say “eggplant” and you are furthest away. {#wangi}
Varma finds all this delightful. Go back far enough, he said, and “even we came from Africa”.

~ He also told of the singer Bade Ghulam Ali Khan, fed only vegetarian food by his hosts for days, who then sang as “but a shadow of himself”. {#ghulam} Ajay Shah answered with George Bernard Shaw’s Caesar, on the barbarian who mistakes his tribe’s customs for the law of nature.

quote.text: He is a barbarian who thinks that the customs of his tribe and island are the law of nature.
quote.who: George Bernard Shaw’s Caesar, as quoted by Ajay Shah

sections.label: The flattening
sections.head: The banana that ate the rest
sections.caption: the Cavendish banana
body: India gave bananas to the world, Amit Varma said, retelling Vikram Doctor. Latin America reduced them to one strain, the yellow Cavendish, which Varma called “boring, monotonous, dull”, and sent it back. {012-S03}
The Cavendish won on economies of scale and shelf life. But India’s hundreds of indigenous bananas are dying out, Doctor laments, and food diversity is under threat.

Pushpesh Pant finds the same at weddings, with one Punjabi stall and one chowmein stall. Yet often, Varma said, within two square kilometres you can find six kinds of biryani, born of six different cuisines. {#biryani}
## Why Varma worries no more

The first burst of markets, he said, brings a drive towards scale and sameness. But deeper markets and decentralising technology now allow a long tail, in food as in Stage’s Haryanvi and Bhojpuri shows.

Ajay Shah, meanwhile, has turned against basmati, the upper-class default among thousands of Indian rice cultivars. Varma, alliterating in Pant’s honour, called it “the barbarism of basmati”. Shah went one better: “brutality of basmati”. {012-J07}
~ In a passage Varma read out, Pant proposes mapping Indian food not by state lines but by souring agent: tamarind or kokum, dried mango or vinegar, star fruit or lime.

quote.text: And this to me has become like a metaphor for the dangers of homogenization.

sections.label: Tongues and towers
sections.head: A dialect with a navy
sections.caption: language, mass media and architecture
body: When radio, television and films arrived, Ajay Shah said, “the beautiful heterogeneity of language did shrink at first”. Many immigrant communities in America converged on one accent, modern standard American English.

North India, he said, never had one Hindustani, only many dialects: a language, after all, is a dialect with a navy. {012-J15} A scant 75 years ago there was no Hindi, and its promotion by the state flattened a people’s language. {#hindi}

Now the tide has turned. “Stage one of electronics is the homogenization of radio and TV, which is mass media,” Shah said. On the internet, people can find Konkani shows, though there are really many Konkanis. {012-C06}
## Built to impress

Architecture, he said, shows the same pull. Powerful people build imposing structures to make the peasants bow. From first principles, a building should suit the local weather, materials and craftsmanship, and still change as technology does. {012-C09}
Shah wants food judged the same way: local, sensible, healthy, and creative rather than aping others.
~ Food culture, he said, should not be a fly in amber. It should evolve with local conditions, preferences and problems.

quote.text: The more totalitarian the regime, the greater their interest in imposing structures.

sections.label: Accidents of history
sections.head: Fuel, teeth and tapioca
sections.caption: why every cuisine is contingent
body: A cuisine, Amit Varma argued, is built in two stages. Local conditions come first: produce, climate, fuel, class and caste. Then the world pours in, and which influences take over is a matter of chance and mimetic desire. {012-C05}

His examples piled up. American PL 480 wheat, shipped during India’s agricultural crisis of the 1960s, brought a little roti culture to the South. {#pl480} A nawab with bad teeth, the legend goes, gave us the melting galouti kebab.
In the middle of the nineteenth century, short of rice, the king of Travancore saw that kappa, or tapioca, was a cheap source of starch. {#kappa} It became part of Kerala’s food culture.
## The flame decides

Fuel mattered too. Old India cooked on cow dung, Vikram Doctor told Varma, and cow dung burns with a low, slow flame, so Indian cuisine was built around boiling. Tandoors and frying came with the Mughals. {012-S06}
Varma added that this is another reason the cow is venerated, which shows how much even religion is circumstantial.

~ Caste split kitchens as well. In the same village, Naren Shenoy observed, Brahmins and Dalits eat very different food. A lot of great non-vegetarian food, Varma added, is eaten lower down the caste ladder.

quote.text: So again, just how something as simple as what is your fuel source can shape an entire cuisine.

sections.label: Culture as party
sections.head: Rabindra rap, anyone?
sections.caption: why culture can’t be appropriated
body: “If it’s cultural, how can there be appropriation?” Amit Varma asked. Culture is the melding of influences, he said, which makes the fashionable phrase cultural appropriation incoherent. {012-C07}

Ajay Shah told what policing culture costs. His friend Rajeswari Sengupta told him that after Rabindranath Tagore died, the owners of his intellectual property demanded his works be performed exactly as in his time. {012-S10}
Shah called it a tragedy, “a cold and pessimistic view of the possibilities of human culture”. He is no friend of rap, he said, “but surely there should be a Rabindra rap sangeet”. {012-J11}
## Shakespeare, remixed

Varma was sure such a thing exists. Shakespeare was never wrapped in cotton wool, he said, so everyone has dug into him: David Gilmour has performed *Sonnet 18*, and the rapper Akala has rapped it. “Culture is all of us having a party,” he said. {012-R24}

~ Shah took the academic view. Culture is all the learned behaviour of Homo sapiens, the software atop the hardware, shared even by Japanese monkeys that learnt to wash sand from their rice. Software can be interrogated and rewritten. {012-C12}

quote.text: Everything that is the software about Homo sapiens is culture.

side.boxText: Pushpesh Pant supplied the pet peeves and *India: Cookbook*. Vikram Doctor, whom Amit Varma calls “the world’s best food writer”, supplied the bananas, the marigolds and the cow dung, in *The Indianness of Indian Food*. {012-R02}

contQuote.text: So it is a plea for preservation. At the same time it’s not a conservative’s plea for stagnation. It’s not a fly in the amber. I don’t want to glorify the past.

p3.title: Stories
p3.deck: A fish, a crop, a dal and a dialect, and what each teaches

stories.start: So salmon sushi we think of as something quintessentially Japanese
stories.end: goes back centuries and is a staple food and all that
stories.caption: Norway’s salmon sushi
stories.kicker: Amit Varma on how a Norwegian glut conquered Japan
stories.head: Something fishy about sushi
body: If Amit Varma orders sushi, salmon is his default. It feels quintessentially Japanese. “But the truth is that salmon sushi as a concept did not exist till the nineteen eighties,” he said. {012-S01}
Norway was harvesting more salmon than it could store and needed export markets. So it sent a man named Bjorn Erik Olsen to Japan to meet the fishery companies.
The Japanese were not keen. The salmon was too pink, not red enough. Local salmon was associated with parasites. An advertising campaign about Norway’s pure waters did not work.

Varma, as a storyteller, imagined the glut spilling into the streets: classrooms so full of salmon that children couldn’t go to school, police stations so full that law and order broke down. A “salmon maximizer”, he called it, like the famous paperclip thought experiment. {#maximizer}

Olsen tried one final, desperate tactic. He went to the food company Nichirei and offered it something like 5,000 or 50,000 tons of salmon, Varma forgot which, at a really cheap price, on condition that it be sold as sushi. {#tons}

Nichirei’s reasoning, in Varma’s telling: “Who can say no to cheap fish?” It took off. Mild salmon, the theory goes, was the sushi most palatable to Western tastes, and this became the point at which sushi went global.
~ Norway’s salmon was saved, the children went back to school, and Japanese sushi was popularised. Ramen, Varma added, is also relatively recent.
stories.why: Dishes that feel ancient are often recent accidents of trade. A Norwegian storage problem made a Japanese dish global, and Varma said it helped Japan as well. Look closely, he said, and pretty much all Indian food is the same. {012-S01}
stories.postscript: Varma apologised to Norwegian viewers for any mispronunciation. He pronounces even Indian and English words wrong, he said, “which are actually the same”.

stories.end: So now you know why cryptocurrency has such a great future in India
stories.caption: Frederick the Great’s potatoes
stories.kicker: Ajay Shah on Frederick the Great and the potato
stories.head: Guard it, and they will steal
body: Grain, Ajay Shah said, citing James C. Scott, is calorie-dense, storable and easy to seize, and Europe’s marauding armies grabbed it from villages. {012-C04} The young Frederick the Great noticed that villagers with potatoes did better. The crop grows underground and looks dirty, and peasants left it in the soil, so armies ignored it.

As king, he pushed the crop, but peasants scorned the nightshade. So, in a story Shah allowed may be apocryphal, Frederick planted potatoes in heavily guarded royal gardens and told the soldiers to look away when people came to steal them.
“This is the best way to make something work,” Shah said. “It is to announce that it is illegal.” {012-S02} Hence, he added, cryptocurrency’s great future in India. {012-J04}
~ In some cases, Shah said, the potato shaped the outcomes of Frederick’s later wars.
stories.why: A crop that is humble and hard to see can be a defence against plunder. And making something look forbidden, Shah suggested, can work better than ordering people to do it.
stories.postscript: Amit Varma called it a brilliant play of incentives, and urged everyone to read Scott’s *Against the Grain*. {012-R10}

stories.start: So I have a little personal story. Uh uh in this room
stories.end: and pull an interesting culture around ourselves every day
stories.caption: his mother’s Osaman
stories.kicker: Ajay Shah on a family recipe that lives only in hands
stories.head: The dal the internet forgot
body: Ajay Shah is half Kutchi and half Kathiawari. Kutchis, he said, will proudly tell you they speak their own language, and many Gujaratis would not follow an authentic Kathiawari conversation.
One tiny subset of Kutchis makes a dal called Osaman, which Shah considers one of the world’s great dals. He has searched the entire internet for his mother’s version. {012-S08} It isn’t there.
So he and his sister plan to film her making it, and he asked the show’s producer, Vartika, on air whether she would take it on.
~ This was a plea for preservation, Shah said, not for stagnation: save the knowledge while you can, then get back to innovating with it. {012-C08}

quote.text: There are some physical motions that she does that can’t be described and it’s just magical how that thing happens.

stories.postscript: Amit Varma recalled Bombay Canteen asking people to mail in their grandmothers’ recipes, then serving them as a day’s menu.

stories.start: I had a great episode with Vinay Single, I've referred to, uh, good guy
stories.end: in my life, I don't have to feel ashamed of my language
stories.caption: Vinay Singhal’s languages
stories.kicker: Amit Varma on Vinay Singhal and the shame of dialect
stories.head: No longer lost in translation
body: Vinay Singhal grew up speaking Haryanvi in a village in Haryana. When he joined a school in town in the ninth standard, Amit Varma said, he found he didn’t know English, and had to learn it from scratch.

Then he moved to a proper big city, and found he had to learn Hindi too. Varma sees the pattern in Maithili and Bhojpuri as well: “The giant monster of Hindi just taking over, destroying you.” {#monster}
Now Singhal’s platform, Stage, streams shows in Haryanvi and other dialects. Kids who watch them come to him with tears in their eyes. {012-S09}
~ Varma called it utterly beautiful. It is also why he no longer frets about homogenisation: a long tail, he argued, needs no economies of scale.

quote.text: For the first time in my life, I don’t have to feel ashamed of my language.

quiz.q: Which country’s glut of fish turned salmon sushi into a global dish in the 1980s?
quiz.a: Norway, which offered Nichirei cheap salmon on condition it be sold as sushi.

quiz.q: How did Frederick the Great, in one possibly apocryphal story, get peasants to grow potatoes?
quiz.a: He guarded royal potato gardens heavily and told soldiers to let thieves through.

quiz.q: Which dish, by Krish Ashok’s theory, came out of a wartime push to eat wheat?
quiz.a: Semolina upma: a kind of wheat that can be cooked like rice.

quiz.q: Why, according to Vikram Doctor, was old Indian cuisine built around boiling food?
quiz.a: Its main fuel was cow dung, which gives a low, slow flame.

quiz.q: What, according to Chinmay Tumbe’s book, is the largest source of internal migration in India?
quiz.a: Marriage: women leave their homes, and often their whole lives, behind.

quiz.q: Which English word, Amit Varma pointed out, comes from Jagannath?
quiz.a: Juggernaut, which to Varma proves English is an Indian language.
